title: Titan Hauling Logistics: straight-line vs double-declining-balance depreciation, asset disposal and book/tax effects
participant_role: Corporate controller at Titan Hauling Logistics advising on depreciation policy and recording a truck sale
judge_role: Chief executive officer (CEO) of Titan Hauling Logistics, who believes accelerated book depreciation saves taxes

difficulty.rationale: Double-declining balance, disposal gain and book vs tax depreciation.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of corporate controller for TITAN HAULING LOGISTICS, an interstate freight trucking company. The chief executive officer (judge) has asked you to explain the company's depreciation choices and to record the sale of a truck.

On January 1, Year 1, Titan bought a heavy-duty freight tractor for $120,000, including delivery and licensing. The tractor has an estimated useful life of 5 years (or 500,000 highway miles) and an estimated salvage value of $20,000. Titan is deciding whether to use the straight-line method or the double-declining-balance method in its financial statements.

The CEO (judge) now wants to replace the tractor with a newer model. Assume Titan uses the double-declining-balance method. On December 31, Year 2, after two full years of service, Titan sells the tractor to an independent operator for $45,000 cash.

The CEO (judge) has heard that faster depreciation helps a company's taxes and wants to know which method is better for Titan.

[Freight tractor data: see exhibits]

You must:
- Compare Year 1 and Year 2 depreciation expense under the straight-line and double-declining-balance methods
- Prepare a schedule showing beginning book value, depreciation, accumulated depreciation and ending book value for both years under each method
- Calculate the gain or loss on the sale of the tractor and record the journal entry
- Explain how the choice of depreciation method affects reported earnings and income taxes

You will present the information to the CEO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the CEO's office. The CEO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the CEO's (judge's) questions, the CEO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Where does the $1,800 gain on disposal appear on Titan's multi-step income statement?
Under the double-declining-balance method, what happens in later years when the formula would drop the book value below the $20,000 salvage value?

solution.overview: A strong answer shows straight-line depreciation of $20,000 a year against double-declining-balance depreciation of $48,000 and $28,800, builds the two-year schedule, and records the sale at a $1,800 gain (book value $43,200). The presenter corrects the tax myth: U.S. tax returns use MACRS whatever book method is chosen, so the book method changes reported earnings and deferred taxes, not cash taxes.

answer: Straight-line: (120,000 minus 20,000) / 5 = $20,000 each year
DDB rate: 1/5 x 2 = 40% of beginning book value; salvage is ignored until the floor is reached
DDB expense is $28,000 higher in Year 1 and $8,800 higher in Year 2
Straight-line: book value 120,000, then 100,000, then 80,000; accumulated depreciation $40,000
DDB: book value 120,000, then 72,000, then 43,200; accumulated depreciation $76,800
Book value = cost minus accumulated depreciation
Both methods stop when book value reaches the $20,000 salvage value
Book value at sale (DDB): 120,000 minus 76,800 = $43,200
Entry: debit Cash and Accumulated Depreciation, credit the Tractor at cost and Gain on Sale
Had Titan used straight-line, book value would be $80,000 and the sale would show a $35,000 loss
DDB lowers reported pre-tax income early ($28,000 lower in Year 1) and raises it later
Over the two years total cost is the same: 120,000 minus 45,000 = $75,000 under either method
U.S. tax depreciation uses MACRS regardless of the book method, so the book choice does not change cash taxes
The difference between book and tax depreciation creates temporary differences recorded as deferred taxes
Choose the book method that best matches how the tractor is used up, not to manage earnings; tell the bank which method is used

calculations.result: $20,000 per year; book value $80,000 after Year 2

calculations.label: Total two-year cost under each method
steps: Both equal cost minus cash received: 120,000 minus 45,000 = $75,000
calculations.result: $75,000 either way; only the timing and labels differ

judge_question_answers.question: Where does the $1,800 gain on disposal appear on Titan's multi-step income statement?
answer: In the Other Revenues and Gains (other income and expense) section, below income from operations
It is kept out of operating revenue because selling used trucks is not Titan's main business
Showing it separately lets users see that operating income did not change because of the sale

judge_question_answers.question: Under the double-declining-balance method, what happens in later years when the formula would drop the book value below the $20,000 salvage value?
answer: An asset is never depreciated below its salvage value
Year 3: 40% x 43,200 = $17,280, leaving a book value of $25,920
Year 4: the formula gives $10,368, which would leave $15,552, so depreciation is limited to 25,920 minus 20,000 = $5,920
Year 5: no depreciation; book value stays at $20,000

key_concepts.definition: Spreading the cost of a long-term asset over the years it is used, to match its cost with the revenue it helps earn.
Equal depreciation each year. Annual depreciation = (cost minus salvage value) / useful life.
An accelerated method. Depreciation = 2 x (1 / useful life) x beginning book value; salvage value is ignored until book value reaches it.
The amount the company expects to get for the asset at the end of its useful life. Book value may not go below it.
A contra-asset account holding all depreciation recorded so far on an asset.
Book value = cost minus accumulated depreciation.
Gain or loss = cash received minus book value at the date of sale. It is reported outside operating income.
The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System, the method required for depreciation on U.S. federal tax returns, no matter which method the financial statements use.
When book and tax depreciation differ, the gap reverses over time and is recorded as a deferred tax asset or liability.
Choosing accounting methods or estimates to make profits look a certain way; methods should reflect economic reality instead.

notes: ICDC level because students must build both schedules, record the disposal and explain the book/tax difference that most students get wrong. Watch for students who subtract salvage value before applying the DDB rate, or who claim the book method lowers cash taxes.
corrections: Corrected the tax claim: Gemini said DDB 'shelters' income and defers cash taxes; in the U.S., tax depreciation uses MACRS regardless of the book method, so the book choice changes reported earnings and creates book/tax (deferred tax) differences, not cash taxes

items.label: Discuss the nature of long-term assets

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the $120,000 tractor (including delivery and licensing) is a long-term asset whose cost is spread over its 5 year useful life to match it with the revenue it helps earn, that book value equals cost minus accumulated depreciation, and that an asset is never depreciated below its $20,000 salvage value.
criteria.meets: Explains that the tractor is recorded at its $120,000 cost and depreciated over its useful life down to, but not below, its $20,000 salvage value.
criteria.below: Describes depreciation vaguely, for example as a drop in market value, or leaves out delivery and licensing as part of cost.
criteria.little: Does not explain what a long-term asset is or why it is depreciated.

items.label: Describe the methods used to value long-term assets

criteria.exceeds: Calculates straight-line depreciation of $20,000 a year and double-declining-balance depreciation at a 40% rate of $48,000 and $28,800, notes DDB is $28,000 higher in Year 1 and $8,800 higher in Year 2, and recommends choosing the method that best matches how the tractor is used up.
criteria.meets: Correctly calculates straight-line depreciation of $20,000 a year and DDB depreciation of $48,000 in Year 1 and $28,800 in Year 2.
criteria.below: Gets straight-line right but makes a DDB error, most often subtracting the $20,000 salvage value before applying the 40% rate (giving $40,000 in Year 1).
criteria.little: Does not calculate depreciation under either method, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

criteria.exceeds: Presents a clear two-year schedule: straight-line book value $120,000, $100,000, $80,000 with $40,000 accumulated depreciation, and DDB book value $120,000, $72,000, $43,200 with $76,800 accumulated depreciation, and explains that both stop at the $20,000 salvage value.
criteria.meets: Shows ending book values of $80,000 (straight-line) and $43,200 (DDB) after Year 2 with the correct accumulated depreciation.
criteria.below: Builds only one method's schedule, or shows a correct expense but wrong book values or accumulated depreciation.
criteria.little: Does not prepare a schedule or track book value.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates the $1,800 gain ($45,000 minus $43,200), shows that straight-line would give a $35,000 loss, proves total two-year cost is $75,000 under either method, and corrects the tax myth: U.S. tax returns use MACRS, so the book method changes reported earnings and deferred taxes, not cash taxes.
criteria.meets: Calculates the $1,800 gain on sale and explains that DDB lowers early reported income but does not change cash taxes because tax depreciation uses MACRS.
criteria.below: Calculates the gain but agrees with the CEO that faster book depreciation lowers taxes, or compares the $45,000 price with the $120,000 cost.
criteria.little: Does not calculate a gain or loss, or gives an unrelated number.

criteria.exceeds: Records the sale (debit Cash $45,000 and Accumulated Depreciation $76,800; credit Freight Tractor $120,000 and Gain on Sale $1,800), shows the entry balances at $121,800, and also gives the $48,000 and $28,800 depreciation entries.
criteria.meets: Records debit Cash $45,000 and Accumulated Depreciation $76,800, credit Freight Tractor $120,000 and Gain on Sale of Equipment $1,800.
criteria.below: Records the entry but leaves out accumulated depreciation, credits the tractor at book value, or has an unbalanced entry.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entry, or an entry with unrelated accounts.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Shows that the method only shifts timing and labels: DDB records $76,800 of depreciation against $40,000 under straight-line but then shows a $1,800 gain instead of a $35,000 loss, so both methods total $75,000.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly that DDB lowers early earnings and raises later earnings without changing total cost.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses the link between depreciation and the gain or loss.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the CEO a clear recommendation to pick the book method that reflects how the tractor wears out, not to manage earnings or taxes, and to tell the bank which method is used.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation on the depreciation method and corrects the CEO's belief about taxes.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation based on the mistaken idea that the book method saves taxes.

criteria.exceeds: Explains depreciation, book value and the book versus tax difference in plain language the CEO can follow, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the schedules, gain calculation and entry clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side schedule or simple visual of the two methods and adds a useful insight such as the $75,000 total cost comparison or the $35,000 loss under straight-line.
criteria.meets: Organizes the two methods in a way that makes the comparison easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: the $1,800 gain goes in Other Revenues and Gains below income from operations because selling trucks is not the main business; and under DDB, Year 3 is $17,280 (book value $25,920), Year 4 is limited to $5,920 so book value stops at $20,000, and Year 5 has no depreciation.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the gain is reported outside operating income and that book value is never depreciated below the $20,000 salvage value.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers such as treating the gain as sales revenue.

key_points: Straight-line: ($120,000 minus $20,000) / 5 = $20,000 a year; book value $80,000 after Year 2
DDB rate 40% of beginning book value (salvage ignored until the floor): $48,000 in Year 1 and $28,800 in Year 2; book value $43,200
Gain on sale = $45,000 minus $43,200 = $1,800 (straight-line would show a $35,000 loss)
Entry: debit Cash $45,000 and Accumulated Depreciation $76,800; credit Freight Tractor $120,000 and Gain on Sale $1,800
Total two-year cost is $75,000 under either method; only timing differs
U.S. tax returns use MACRS regardless of the book method, so the book choice does not change cash taxes; differences create deferred taxes
Book value is never depreciated below the $20,000 salvage value
